name: Catherine of Aragon
role: Queen of England as Henry VIII's first wife (1509–1533); regent during the 1513 war with Scotland
summary: Spanish-born queen who was married to Henry VIII until the marriage was annulled by the English church in 1533. Her surviving words and her record show a devout Catholic who refused the royal supremacy, appealed her case toward Rome and governed England as regent in 1513. Little of her own writing sets out a general political programme.

sources.title: The Life of Cardinal Wolsey (George Cavendish; Project Gutenberg text)
sources.author: George Cavendish
sources.usedFor: Her 1529 speech at the Blackfriars legatine court, as reported by Cavendish (secondhand, written decades later): appeal for justice, distrust of English counsel, wish for counsel from Spain

sources.title: Catherine of Aragon
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Overview of her record: 1513 regency and Scottish war, 1520 advice on alliance, refusal of the royal supremacy, poor relief, religious devotion, 1536 letter (authenticity disputed)

sources.title: Letters and Papers, Foreign and Domestic, Henry VIII, vol. 1 (September 1513 despatches)
sources.author: J. S. Brewer (ed.), British History Online
sources.usedFor: Context for the 1513 war with Scotland and the Flodden despatches; no statement by her was taken from this page

more-religion-public.rationale: Inferred: she put the marriage question under the Church's law and the Pope's jurisdiction against the king's courts (Cavendish), which suggests she wanted religious authority to weigh more in public decisions.

gradual-change.rationale: Her record: she refused the annulment and the break from Rome and appealed to the established Church and the Pope against the king's changes, which is clearly implied by what she did (Cavendish; Wikipedia).

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Her record: she urged Henry to ally with her nephew Charles V rather than with France in 1520 (Wikipedia), which is a stated preference for a continuing foreign alliance.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Her record: she refused to accept Henry as supreme head of the Church in England and kept to papal authority over her marriage, opposing the king's control of the Church (Wikipedia, citing the 1533 events). Her position is shown by that refusal rather than a quoted statement.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: In her speech at the 1529 Blackfriars court she asked that the case be decided by the law and not by the king's pleasure ('if there be any just cause by the law that ye can allege against me'), reported by Cavendish, which is secondhand.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Inferred: she refused to accept the 1533 annulment and the royal supremacy that Parliament enacted (Wikipedia), which suggests she did not accept Parliament as the final authority on Church and marriage matters.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Her record: as queen she started an extensive programme for the relief of the poor and gave to colleges and charities (Wikipedia), which shows she accepted that the privileged owe care to the less fortunate.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Cavendish reports that she asked for counsel from Spain, not England, saying her English judges could not be indifferent, and that the case should be heard in Rome; this is secondhand and her words are only partly quoted.

religion-illusion.rationale: Her record: she was a devout Catholic who prayed and gave her life to religious duty and called her soul the first concern (Wikipedia, citing the 1536 letter, whose authenticity is disputed). Her devotion implies she rejected the view that religion is an illusion.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Her record: she urged Henry to enter an alliance with Charles V rather than with France (Wikipedia), a preference for taking a side between the great powers.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Inferred: she pressed for the rights of her daughter Mary, the heir presumptive, and asked Charles V to protect her (Wikipedia), which suggests she accepted succession by a ruler's child.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Inferred: she refused to accept the annulment and the new court's authority in conscience, which suggests she did not treat a law she thought unjust as binding on her conscience (Cavendish; Wikipedia).

notes: Early-exit audit: her recorded political positions are few. Her own words survive mainly in letters about her marriage and her daughter, and in Cavendish's account of her 1529 speech, which is secondhand. Most statements are null. Her appeal to Rome and her refusal of the royal supremacy are the clearest public positions. Several answers are low-confidence inferences from those positions. Her 1536 letter to Henry is reported by later writers and its authenticity is disputed, so it is not used as an answer.
